B01:
Choose wrong between RAG and fine-tuning and you pay in wasted build time and wrong answers. The two approaches solve different problems.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation pulls answers from a live knowledge base at query time. That buys you freshness and citations: the model can reference current documents and point users to the exact source. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge and tone into the model's weights, which buys you style and latency. Responses come back fast and consistent, with no retrieval step in the path.

Say you run a customer-support knowledge base with 100,000 documents. If the content changes often and users expect source links, retrieval wins. If tone and response speed matter more, tuning does. The trade-offs below cover the cases in between, including when to use both.
B02:
Teams treat indexes as the cure for slow Postgres queries: a query drags, someone adds an index and moves on. The bill lands on the write side. Each INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE must maintain each index on the table, whether or not any query ever reads it.

Unused indexes are the most overlooked version of this cost. An index that serves no queries still bloats your writes, and it inflates storage and stretches vacuum cycles on top.

A recent client showed how far this drifts. One core table had accumulated 23 indexes over the years. We audited them and dropped 14. Write throughput doubled, on the same hardware, with the same queries.

The pitfalls below are the ones we see most, along with how to find unused indexes in your own database and a checklist for keeping them lean.

T01:
I sent thousands of cold emails last year and ended at an 8% reply rate.

Five lessons carried most of that: 🧵

1/ Keep it to 4 lines. Your prospect is scanning on a phone between meetings, and four lines covers who you are, why you're relevant, and what you want. Longer gets archived.

2/ One CTA per email. Each added ask cuts your reply rate. "Worth a 15-min chat?" beats a menu of options.

3/ Personalize the first line with something you read and can say one specific thing about. One specific sentence beats five templated ones.

4/ Follow up. Most of my replies came from the 2nd or 3rd email. A polite bump reads as persistence, and silence is not a no.

5/ Track subject lines, send times, and CTAs, and iterate each week. The 8% came after I started treating cold email as a system instead of a lottery.
T02: Most meetings should be memos. Writing forces clarity and leaves a record you can search. An idea that can't survive being written down won't survive a 60-minute meeting either.
T03:
19 months ago I launched a $49 one-time product.

This week we crossed $10k MRR, with no funding and no team.

The bootstrapped playbook, in 4 tweets: 🧵

1/ Start ugly. V1 was a $49 one-time purchase, no dashboard, a bare landing page. A handful of sales proved people would pay, and that proof mattered more than polish.

2/ Listen for the pivot. Customers kept returning with the same recurring problem, and a one-time product couldn't serve it. In month 7 we moved to subscriptions. Revenue dipped for a few weeks, then compounded.

3/ Do things that don't scale. I onboarded each early customer myself, answered each support email, and asked churned users why they left. We built the roadmap straight from those conversations.

4/ 19 months to $10k MRR is slow, and slow worked: profitable, compounding growth on our own terms. If you're bootstrapping, keep going. It adds up.

T05:
A new paper puts LLM-as-judge to the test against human raters.

The findings, in 4 tweets: 🧵

1/ LLM judges agree with human evaluators 81% of the time overall. For routine evaluation tasks, that makes an LLM judge a reasonable stand-in for a human rater.

2/ On creative tasks, agreement drops to 64%. Style, originality, taste: once no single correct answer exists, LLM judges and human raters part ways.

3/ The authors suggest a cause: judges reward surface features like structure, fluency, and length, and originality registers in none of those.

4/ Use LLM judges for scale on objective tasks, and keep humans in the loop for creative work. 81% agreement is workable. 64% sits close to a coin flip.

R01: Automated code review promises lower defect rates and lighter reviewer workload, yet existing tools remain limited in scope and precision. We present ReviewBot, an automated code-review system that combines static analysis with learned models to surface defects within the pull-request workflow. We evaluate ReviewBot on 1,200 pull requests drawn from 8 repositories that span multiple languages and project sizes. ReviewBot caught 34% more defects than baseline linters while maintaining a 12% false-positive rate, a level the developers in our study described as acceptable for day-to-day use. Analysis by defect category shows the largest gains on cross-file inconsistencies and API-misuse patterns that escape traditional linters. We also examine deployment considerations at scale, including reviewer trust, alert fatigue, and integration with continuous-integration pipelines. Our findings support automated review as a complement to human reviewers. We outline future work on adaptive precision thresholds and repository-specific tuning, and we release our evaluation framework to support reproducibility.
R02:
We surveyed 156 enterprises across industries and regions about their data-governance practices, challenges, and priorities.

We found a wide maturity gap. Of the enterprises surveyed, 44% have no data-classification policy, which leaves them unable to say which data is sensitive, regulated, or business-critical. Without classification as a foundation, downstream controls such as access management, retention, encryption, and incident response rest on guesswork.

Organizations that lack this foundation report longer audit cycles, higher breach-response costs, and growing friction as AI initiatives demand well-understood, well-labeled data.

To close the gap, this whitepaper recommends a 5-step maturity model that takes organizations from initial data discovery through classification, ownership, policy enforcement, and continuous monitoring. Each step includes concrete milestones and self-assessment criteria for benchmarking progress.

Enterprises that classify their data move faster, and with less risk, on compliance, security, and AI adoption than those still deciding where to start.
R03:
Pilot firms running AI-assisted contract review report review time down 60%. Work that consumed days of associate attention now takes hours, and legal teams spend the difference on negotiation strategy and higher-value counsel. Legal ops leaders under pressure to do more with less have noticed.

One caveat deserves equal billing: hallucinated citations. AI tools can produce authorities that look plausible and do not exist, and courts have shown little patience with filings that include them. Qualified human review of each AI-assisted output remains the rule.

The profession's guardrails are forming. The ABA has issued guidance on lawyers' use of generative AI, stressing competence, confidentiality, and supervision: adopt the technology, own the output.

For legal teams starting now: begin with high-volume, lower-risk workflows like contract review, measure the results, and keep lawyers in the loop. Firms that pair AI's speed with a lawyer's judgment will set the standard for what legal service becomes.
